periods.title: Exploring Pyramids of Giza
periods.text: Begin your day at Pyramids of Giza early to beat the crowds and catch the best light. The main site is most atmospheric in the morning when the air is cool and the landscape catches the first golden rays. Take time to explore the main highlights and capture photographs in the soft morning light. This is the most rewarding time to visit.
periods.tip: Arrive as early as possible — the first hour after opening has the fewest visitors and the best photography conditions.

periods.title: Deeper Exploration
periods.text: Spend the afternoon exploring further afield. Explore the surrounding areas, museums, or lesser-known sections that most visitors miss. Grab lunch at a local eatery for authentic flavours and budget-friendly prices.
periods.tip: Midday sun can be intense — bring sunscreen, a hat, and plenty of water. Rest during the hottest hours if needed.

periods.title: Golden Hour & Farewell
periods.text: End the day watching the golden hour transform the landscape. The evening light at Pyramids of Giza is spectacular and worth waiting for. Find a local restaurant for dinner — local specialities at honest prices.
periods.tip: Sunset times vary by season — check ahead and position yourself 30 minutes early for the best spot.

3.title: Pyramids of Giza — The Classic Icons

periods.title: Great Pyramid & the Sphinx
periods.text: Arrive at the Giza Plateau at opening (8am) to beat the tour buses. Buy a ticket that includes access to the interior of the Great Pyramid of Khufu — the ascending corridor and King's Chamber are genuinely awe-inspiring. Spend the first hour moving between all three pyramids on the main plateau and then loop down to the Great Sphinx and the Valley Temple of Khafre for close-up views of the limestone causeway.
periods.tip: Interior pyramid tickets sell out — book at the ticket office the moment it opens, or pre-book through an official tour operator.

periods.title: Solar Boat Museum
periods.text: On the south side of the Great Pyramid sits the Solar Boat Museum, housing a 4,600-year-old cedar funerary barque reassembled from 1,200 pieces. It's one of the oldest intact vessels on earth. Afterwards, hire a camel or horse for a ride to the panoramic viewpoint on the desert ridge southwest of the plateau — this is where the classic "three pyramids in a line" photograph is taken. Grab lunch at a restaurant on Nazlet El-Semman street.
periods.tip: The panoramic desert ridge is a 10-minute ride from the main gate — agree a fixed price with your camel handler before setting off.

periods.title: Sound & Light Show
periods.text: The Sound & Light Show runs on the Giza Plateau most evenings after dark, projecting coloured light onto the pyramids and Sphinx while a narration recounts ancient Egyptian history. It's theatrical and unmistakably touristy — but watching the illuminated Sphinx narrate its own story in the desert night air is a genuinely memorable experience. Book tickets in advance as shows sell out in peak season.
periods.tip: Check the language schedule ahead — shows cycle through Arabic, English, French, and other languages on different evenings.

periods.title: Saqqara Necropolis
periods.text: Take a taxi or guided tour 30km south to Saqqara, the vast ancient burial ground that predates Giza by centuries. The centrepiece is the Step Pyramid of Djoser — the world's oldest monumental stone structure, built around 2650 BCE. Unlike Giza, Saqqara sees far fewer visitors, so you can wander the mortuary complex and painted interior chambers of the Pyramid of Teti with genuine solitude. The site stretches for kilometres and rewards slow exploration.
periods.tip: Combine Saqqara and Memphis in a single day trip — most taxis will wait while you visit both sites for a fixed half-day rate.

periods.title: Ancient Capital of Memphis
periods.text: A short drive from Saqqara, the open-air museum at Mit Rahina marks the site of Memphis, the original capital of unified Egypt. The highlight is a colossal limestone statue of Ramesses II — 10 metres long and laid on its back after its legs broke off — displayed in its own building. The alabaster sphinx in the garden is smaller than Giza's but better preserved. The surrounding palm groves and quietness make it feel like a genuine discovery.
periods.tip: Memphis is often skipped by tour groups in favour of Saqqara — arrive after 2pm and you may have the statues almost entirely to yourself.

periods.title: Dinner in Giza City
periods.text: Return to Giza or Cairo for the evening and explore the local neighbourhood restaurants away from the tourist strip. The area around El Haram Street has traditional Egyptian kushary joints — a comforting dish of rice, lentils, pasta, and spiced tomato sauce that costs almost nothing. Wash it down with fresh sugarcane juice from a street vendor. This is the side of Cairo that most visitors staying in hotel restaurants never see.
periods.tip: Kushary is best at dedicated kushary restaurants — look for busy local spots with workers queuing at the counter at dinner time.

periods.title: Grand Egyptian Museum
periods.text: The Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM) in Giza, adjacent to the pyramids plateau, houses the complete treasures of Tutankhamun — over 5,000 artefacts including the iconic gold death mask, chariot, and gilded throne. The Royal Mummy Room displays over 20 pharaonic mummies. Arrive at opening to avoid school groups. Even a partial visit through the Tutankhamun galleries and the Atrium Hall with its colossal Ramesses II statue justifies the entry fee.
periods.tip: Book GEM tickets online in advance — walk-in queues can exceed 90 minutes on busy days, especially during Egyptian school holidays.

periods.title: Khan el-Khalili Bazaar
periods.text: Cairo's medieval bazaar has been trading since the 14th century. Khan el-Khalili is a warren of souks selling spices, perfume oils, lanterns, papyrus, jewellery, and hand-beaten copper. The surrounding lanes of the Al-Hussein neighbourhood are as interesting as the market itself — the Al-Azhar Mosque is free to enter and stunning. Drink a glass of mint tea at El Fishawy cafe, which claims to have operated without closing for over 200 years.
periods.tip: Bargaining is expected — start at 40–50% of the first asking price and negotiate from there. Walk away slowly if the price won't shift.

periods.title: Nile Felucca & Farewell Dinner
periods.text: End your final evening with a sunset felucca ride on the Nile — the traditional wooden sailboats have been carrying passengers along the river for millennia. Negotiate an hour-long sunset trip from the Corniche El Nil embankment. Afterwards, head to one of the riverfront restaurants near Zamalek or Garden City for a farewell dinner of grilled kofta, ful medames, and Egyptian flatbread while watching the lights of Cairo reflect in the water.
periods.tip: Fix the felucca price before boarding — a one-hour sunset ride for a small group should cost 100–200 EGP total, not per person.

budgetTips.title: Book ahead online
budgetTips.text: Tickets and tours booked online are often 10-30% cheaper than walk-in prices. Many attractions sell out in peak season — advance booking guarantees entry and saves money.

budgetTips.title: Visit in shoulder season
budgetTips.text: Shoulder months (just before or after peak season) offer better prices on accommodation and flights with similar weather and fewer crowds. Oct – Apr is peak.

budgetTips.title: Stay nearby, not at the gate
budgetTips.text: Accommodation directly at the attraction charges a premium. Staying 10-20 minutes away can save 30-50% on nightly rates. Use public transport or a rental car to bridge the gap.

budgetTips.title: Pack your own lunch
budgetTips.text: Tourist-area restaurants charge inflated prices. Pack sandwiches, snacks, and a refillable water bottle to save $15-30 per day on food. Buy supplies at local supermarkets or markets.

budgetTips.title: Free walking tours & guides
budgetTips.text: Many areas offer free or tip-based guided walks that are better than paid tours. Local guides provide insider knowledge and support the community. Check online for options.

budgetTips.title: Use local transport
budgetTips.text: Taxis and private transfers are the most expensive option. Local buses, shared minivans, or ride-sharing are 50-80% cheaper and give you a more authentic experience.

budgetBreakdown.notes: Street food → local restaurants → fine dining
Public buses → shared transfers → private car

practicalInfo.title: Entry & Visas
items: Keep a digital and physical copy of your passport, visa, and travel insurance at all times
Entry fees for Pyramids of Giza should be paid in EGP — exchange money before arriving

practicalInfo.title: Health & Safety
items: Check malaria prophylaxis requirements — some areas require medication
Bring a basic first aid kit with blister plasters, antiseptic, painkillers, and any personal medication
Sun protection is essential — apply SPF 50+ and reapply every 2 hours

practicalInfo.title: Getting Around
items: Shared transport or guided tours are the most practical options
Download offline maps before arriving — mobile data coverage can be patchy in remote areas
Negotiate transport prices before departure or use metered taxis and ride-hailing apps

practicalInfo.title: Connectivity
items: Buy a local SIM card at the airport on arrival for affordable data — much cheaper than international roaming
WiFi is available at most accommodation but signal quality varies. Download offline maps and guides before heading to remote areas
Share your itinerary with someone at home and check in daily, especially for remote treks or island visits

practicalInfo.title: Money
items: Currency: EGP (Pound). Cards accepted in tourist areas, but carry cash for local vendors
ATMs are available in larger towns but can be unreliable — withdraw enough cash before heading to remote areas
Tip 10-15% at restaurants. Guides and porters appreciate tips — budget $5-10 per day per person

practicalInfo.title: Packing Tips
items: Comfortable walking shoes, layers for temperature changes, and a packable rain jacket
A reusable water bottle, headlamp, and portable phone charger are essential for any outdoor adventure
Quick-dry clothing is ideal — you can wash and wear repeatedly, reducing pack weight

culturalTips.title: Respect Local Customs
culturalTips.text: Be mindful of local customs and traditions. Ask before photographing people. Learn basic greetings in the local language — even a simple hello earns goodwill.

culturalTips.title: Leave No Trace
culturalTips.text: Pack out all rubbish. Stay on marked trails and paths. Do not touch, feed, or disturb wildlife. The natural beauty of Pyramids of Giza depends on every visitor treating it with respect. Take only photos, leave only footprints.

culturalTips.title: Photography Etiquette
culturalTips.text: Ask permission before photographing locals, especially in indigenous or traditional communities. Many religious sites have photography restrictions — check signage and respect these rules. Drone regulations vary — check local laws before flying.

culturalTips.title: Language & Communication
culturalTips.text: Learn a few words in Arabic — greetings, please, thank you, and numbers go a long way. English is limited outside tourist areas but a translation app helps bridge gaps.

culturalTips.title: Support Local Communities
culturalTips.text: Choose locally-owned guesthouses, restaurants, and guides over international chains. Buy handicrafts directly from artisans. Your spending has the most impact when it goes directly into the local economy rather than through large tour operators.

culturalTips.title: Pace & Patience
culturalTips.text: Things move at a different pace here — embrace it. Delays, diversions, and unexpected encounters are part of the adventure. Patience and flexibility will transform your experience.
